notes:
Task and constraints: Count ordered boomerang triples where two distinct endpoints are at equal distance from each pivot point.
Idea: For each pivot, count other points by squared Euclidean distance and add v(v-1) for each distance group.
Technique and why it applies: Any two distinct points in a group can occupy the second and third tuple positions in either order, giving v choices followed by v-1 choices.
Invariant: group[d] stores the number of non-pivot points at squared distance d from the current pivot.
Edge cases: The code explicitly skips the pivot itself. Distinct points are guaranteed, and squared distance avoids floating-point square roots.
Complexity: Each pivot scans all points and then its distance groups, giving O(n²) expected time and O(n) temporary map space.

Task and constraints: Return all values in [1,n] missing from an array whose entries lie in that range.
Idea: Mark each value's target index negative, then collect indices that remain positive.
Technique and why it applies: The absolute value maps a possibly negated entry back to its value; negating nums[value-1] records that the value appeared. The second pass identifies unmarked positions.
Invariant: After the marking pass, a negative entry at index i means i+1 appeared in the input.
Edge cases: The second pass restores every negative entry to positive, so the input's original values are preserved. Values must remain within [1,n].
Complexity: Two linear passes give O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space excluding the result list, matching the labels.

Task and constraints: Rearrange characters of s in descending order of character frequency.
Idea: Count characters, push negative frequencies and characters into a min-heap, then append each character its frequency number of times.
Technique and why it applies: Negative counts make the smallest heap key correspond to the largest frequency. Equal frequencies are secondarily ordered by character because heap entries are tuples.
Invariant: Each heap entry represents one distinct character and its total count; result contains all entries already popped and expanded.
Edge cases: The snippet uses Counter and heapq without importing either name, so it fails unless those names are supplied externally. Empty input would return an empty string if imports exist.
Complexity: Counting is O(n), heap construction by repeated pushes is O(u log u), and output construction emits n characters. Total time is O(n+u log u), with O(u+n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum arrows needed to burst intervals representing balloon horizontal spans.
Idea: Sort intervals and merge each overlapping group by maintaining the common intersection of their endpoints.
Technique and why it applies: If the next interval starts at or before the current intersection's right edge, one arrow can burst both, so the right edge shrinks to the smaller endpoint. A disjoint interval starts a new arrow group.
Invariant: ans contains one intersection interval for each group of balloons that can share an arrow.
Edge cases: The code assumes points is nonempty because it initializes ans from points[0]. It sorts the input list in place. Endpoints are inclusive, so touching spans overlap.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), and the merging scan is O(n). The ans list may store O(n) intersections, so auxiliary storage is O(n).

Task and constraints: Return the minimum number of arrows that intersect all balloon intervals.
Idea: Sort intervals and greedily form groups with a shared intersection, counting one arrow per group.
Technique and why it applies: The algorithm starts with the first interval's right endpoint and narrows right_bound as long as following intervals start no later than it. When an interval is disjoint, the current group is complete and another arrow is counted.
Invariant: right_bound is the right edge of the common intersection for the current group.
Edge cases: Empty points returns zero. The sorted intervals are processed in place; touching endpoints are considered overlapping by <=.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), followed by a linear scan. Explicit auxiliary space is O(1), though Python sorting may use temporary memory.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of moves to make all array values equal when a move increments n-1 elements by one.
Idea: Use the equivalent operation of decrementing one element and subtract the minimum value from every element conceptually.
Technique and why it applies: Each move increases all but one value, which has the same effect on relative differences as decreasing the excluded value. Reducing all values to the minimum therefore needs the sum of each value's excess over that minimum.
Invariant: sum(nums)-min(nums)*len(nums) equals the total excess above the minimum.
Edge cases: The solution assumes nums is nonempty because min(nums) is used. A single-element array returns zero.
Complexity: sum and min each scan the array, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Calculate the fewest moves needed to equalize an integer array under the increment-n-1-elements operation.
Idea: Compute total sum minus array length times the minimum value.
Technique and why it applies: Incrementing all but one element is equivalent, in terms of differences, to decrementing just one element. The optimal target is the minimum value, so every other element contributes its excess to the move count.
Invariant: The expression sums nums[i]-minimum over all entries without modifying the input.
Edge cases: nums must be nonempty for min(nums) to be defined. A singleton yields zero moves.
Complexity: Both sum and min are O(n), while only a few scalar values are stored, so O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space match the labels.

Task and constraints: Count index tuples whose four selected values sum to zero, with each index drawn from a different array.
Idea: Count pair sums from nums1 and nums2, count pair sums from nums3 and nums4, and match opposite sums.
Technique and why it applies: Every pair from the first two arrays contributes to a frequency map. For each sum s in that map, n1n2[s] times n3n4[-s] gives the number of complementary index pairs.
Invariant: Each map records the number of index pairs producing its key sum.
Edge cases: The code uses defaultdict without importing it, so it fails unless that name is defined externally. Zero-valued sums and duplicate values are handled by their frequencies.
Complexity: Pair-sum construction is O(n²) for each side and matching is O(n²) worst case, giving O(n²) time and O(n²) space for arrays of length n.

Task and constraints: Count quadruples, one value from each of four arrays, whose sum is zero.
Idea: Build a frequency counter for sums from A and B, then query the counter for the negated sums from C and D.
Technique and why it applies: For each pair (c,d), every A,B pair summing to -(c+d) forms one valid quadruple, so the counter frequency is added to the result.
Invariant: A_B_sum[x] is the number of index pairs from A and B that sum to x.
Edge cases: Duplicate values and sums are correctly counted by Counter frequencies. The method assumes the arrays have compatible lengths but does not require them to be equal.
Complexity: Building pair sums and iterating the other pair combinations take O(n²) time, with O(n²) counter storage for equal-length arrays.

Task and constraints: Maximize the number of children whose greed factors can be satisfied by assigning each child at most one cookie.
Idea: Sort greed factors and cookie sizes, then assign the smallest adequate cookie to the least greedy unserved child.
Technique and why it applies: If a cookie is too small, it cannot satisfy the current child or any later child with greater or equal greed, so the cookie pointer advances. Otherwise both pointers advance and the satisfied count increases.
Invariant: The first c children in sorted order have been satisfied with distinct cookies among those processed.
Edge cases: Empty child or cookie lists return zero. Sorting mutates both input lists.
Complexity: Sorting dominates at O(g log g+s log s); the two-pointer pass is O(g+s). Auxiliary space is O(1) beyond sorting implementation and inputs.

Task and constraints: Assign cookies to as many children as possible without giving any child more than one cookie.
Idea: Sort children by greed and cookies by size, then scan cookies from smallest to largest.
Technique and why it applies: Each cookie that meets the least unserved child's greed is assigned to that child. Smaller cookies are skipped because they cannot satisfy that child, and later children are no less demanding.
Invariant: i points to the least greedy child not yet satisfied; result counts assignments already made.
Edge cases: If g is empty, the first cookie iteration breaks immediately; if s is empty, the loop returns zero. Both lists are sorted in place.
Complexity: Sorting is O(g log g+s log s) and the scan is O(g+s). The explicit extra variables use O(1) space, consistent with the author label aside from sort temporaries.

Task and constraints: Determine whether there are indices i<j<k with nums[i]<nums[k]<nums[j], the 132 pattern.
Idea: Scan from right to left, keeping a decreasing stack of candidates for the middle value and a saved candidate for the '2' value.
Technique and why it applies: Popping values smaller than the current number updates third to a value that can serve as nums[k] beneath a larger nums[j]. If an earlier number is less than third, the required triple exists.
Invariant: third is the best known middle-position candidate value for a pattern whose first element may still be found to its left.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return False. Duplicate values do not satisfy the strict inequalities because the final test uses <.
Complexity: Each value is pushed once and popped at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

Task and constraints: Detect whether the array contains a 132 subsequence with strictly ordered indices and values.
Idea: For each prospective third index k, scan all earlier values and remember whether a smaller value has appeared before a later larger-than-current value.
Technique and why it applies: valid becomes True when an earlier value is below nums[k]; if a subsequent earlier value exceeds nums[k] while valid is true, those values form a 132 pattern in index order.
Invariant: During the inner loop, valid records whether some earlier value is smaller than the candidate third value.
Edge cases: The code returns False for arrays too short to form a triple. It only compares values before k, so the earlier smaller and middle candidate both precede the third index.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(n²) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching the author labels.

Task and constraints: Return True if nums contains a 132 pattern and False otherwise.
Idea: Scan backward with a monotonic stack and track ak, a candidate value for the pattern's '2'.
Technique and why it applies: When the current value exceeds stack-top values, those popped values can serve as the third element while the current value is the middle element. A later scan value smaller than ak completes the pattern.
Invariant: ak stores a feasible third value associated with a middle value to its right, and stk stores unresolved decreasing candidates.
Edge cases: The pattern requires three distinct positions and strict inequalities; the test nums[i] < ak enforces the final strict comparison. Short inputs return False.
Complexity: Each number is pushed and popped at most once, so time is O(n) and stack space O(n), consistent with labels.

Task and constraints: Detect a cycle in a circular array where every step in the cycle must have the same direction and length greater than one.
Idea: Start from every index, follow the computed next index, and track visited positions plus the minimum and maximum step values.
Technique and why it applies: The index formula wraps jumps modulo n while preserving large jump distances. A cycle is accepted only if it returns to its starting index, has more than one position, and all visited values share a sign.
Invariant: seen contains indices in the current traversal, while minval and maxval summarize direction signs encountered.
Edge cases: The code assumes nums is nonempty and values are nonzero as specified. A one-index cycle is rejected by len(seen)>1; mixed signs fail the sign test.
Complexity: A fresh set and traversal are started for each index, so worst-case time can be O(n²) and auxiliary space O(n), unlike linear methods that mark visited paths globally.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a circular array has a cycle of length greater than one with all jumps in the same direction.
Idea: Use Floyd's slow/fast pointers to detect a cycle while checking that each jump's sign matches the starting direction.
Technique and why it applies: next_index wraps indices around the array. The loop stops when a step changes sign; if slow and fast meet, a one-element self-loop is rejected and any longer cycle is accepted. Afterwards, the traversed path is zero-marked to avoid reprocessing it.
Invariant: During each detection run, all followed jumps have the same sign as nums[i].
Edge cases: nums[i]==0 is skipped because zero marks an already processed position. The method mutates nums, and modulo behavior supports negative jumps.
Complexity: Each index is zero-marked at most once, giving O(n) total time and O(1) auxiliary space, consistent with the labels.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum pigs needed to identify one poisonous bucket within the testing time, given the time to observe a death.
Idea: Treat each pig as having one more distinguishable outcome than the number of complete test rounds and increase the pig count until outcomes cover all buckets.
Technique and why it applies: With t rounds, each pig can encode t+1 states, so p pigs distinguish (t+1)^p bucket patterns. The loop finds the smallest p reaching the bucket count.
Invariant: req_pigs is the smallest tested count not yet known to provide enough patterns; it increments until the capacity threshold is met.
Edge cases: minutesToDie must be positive. The floating-point division can introduce rounding for large values, though usual constraints are small.
Complexity: The loop performs O(log_buckets) iterations for a fixed number of outcomes per pig and uses O(1) space. The capacity calculation uses floating-point arithmetic.

Task and constraints: Check whether a string is formed by repeating a shorter nonempty substring at least twice.
Idea: Try each candidate substring length up to half the full string length and compare repeated copies with s.
Technique and why it applies: A repeated pattern's unit length must divide the total length. The code constructs s[:i] repeated len(s)//i times and returns True when the result equals s.
Invariant: Each failed iteration rules out one possible unit length; all possible proper lengths are tested by the end.
Edge cases: A single-character string returns False because there is no candidate length. The code only tests lengths that can repeat at least twice.
Complexity: There are O(n) candidate lengths and each comparison constructs/scans O(n) characters, giving O(n²) time and O(n) temporary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether s consists of multiple copies of a smaller substring.
Idea: Build a KMP prefix table and use the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix to infer the repeated unit length.
Technique and why it applies: If the final prefix value is j, the candidate period is len(s)-j-1. A nonempty border and divisibility of the string length by that period indicate repetition.
Invariant: prefix[i] stores the index of the final character of the longest proper prefix matching a suffix ending at i.
Edge cases: A string with no nonempty proper border returns False. Empty strings are outside the usual constraints because the final expression indexes prefix[-1].
Complexity: Prefix construction scans the string with fallback links, taking O(n) time and O(n) space, consistent with the labels.

Task and constraints: Count bit positions where integers x and y differ.
Idea: XOR the integers, then count the set bits in the result.
Technique and why it applies: XOR produces a one exactly where corresponding bits differ. Repeatedly clearing the lowest set bit with z &= z-1 counts one differing position per iteration.
Invariant: ans equals the number of set bits already removed from z.
Edge cases: Equal integers yield z=0 and return zero. The solution assumes the integer representation used by the problem, normally nonnegative values.
Complexity: The loop runs once per set bit, O(w) worst case for w-bit integers, with O(1) auxiliary space.
